intro.hook: Uy, may lakad ka ba this weekend?
intro.hookTranslation: Hey, got any plans this weekend?
intro.title: Sound natural, not textbook
intro.subtitle: In about 2 minutes, you’ll learn to:

goals.meaning: Use the little words locals add

goals.tagalog: Wala pa naman. Bakit, may lakad ka?
goals.meaning: Answer like a friend, not a textbook

steps.title: Tiny words, big difference
steps.body: Locals soften sentences with tiny words that textbooks skip. That’s why textbook Tagalog sounds stiff.
steps.footnote: Pa means “yet”, naman softens the answer, and lang means “just”.

steps.audio: Uy, may lakad ka ba this weekend?
steps.note: Lakad means “walk”, but between friends it means plans or an outing. Switching to English mid-sentence is totally normal in Manila.

steps.contextTranslation: What are your plans for Saturday?

options.text: Ako ay walang plano sa Sabado.
options.translation: I have no plans on Saturday.
options.explanation: Correct, but the ay order sounds like a speech. Friends never talk like this.

options.text: Wala pa naman. Bakit, may lakad ka?
options.translation: Nothing yet. Why, got something in mind?
options.explanation: Pa and naman keep it relaxed, and you toss the question back. This is how friends answer.
Fine grammar, but it sounds like you don’t want to talk.

steps.title: Say it like a local
steps.display: Wala pa naman. Bakit, may lakad ka?
steps.translation: Nothing yet. Why, got something in mind?
steps.target: Wala pa naman bakit may lakad ka
steps.tip: Let it flow as one breath: wa-la-pa-na-MAN.

turns.buddy: Tara, kain tayo ng samgyup sa Sabado!
turns.buddyTranslation: Let’s eat Korean barbecue on Saturday!

closing.translation: Seven o’clock, on Maginhawa Street. See you!

completion.title: That’s how friends talk!
completion.subtitle: You picked the natural reply and settled a time and place.
